extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers studying scientific method, classification, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and theoretical principles for creating and evaluating scientific classifications (taxonomies) that reveal real correlations among properties and enable deduction and prediction. Emphasises logical form (bifurcate classification), empirical verification, and avoidance of irrelevant 'accidents'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural classification / correlation of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural class is one 'disclosing many general laws connecting together the physical and mechanical properties of the substances classified' — grouping in which the correlation of properties is most conspicuously manifested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arrangements where knowledge of the primary form allows inference of other properties (example: crystals of the regular system — knowing the cube form permits inference of equal elasticity, absence of double refraction, equal thermal expansion). A good classification reveals empirical laws and connections rather than merely grouping by superficial resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical basis and hypothesis verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification must be founded upon empirical observation and is strengthened when accompanied by a 'Descriptive Hypothesis' that explains and is experimentally verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses (e.g. crystalline axes hypothesis) to apply deductive reasoning and test predictions (Mitscherlich's prediction about temperature reducing double refraction; Savart's experimental verification of varying elasticity). Classifications that harmonise with experiment are superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive grouping as logical ideal (but impracticable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The logically perfect rule would be to group given objects in every possible way and choose the grouping that best manifests correlations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise this is usually impracticable (combinatorial explosion). Do not attempt exhaustive enumeration for large sets; instead proceed by heuristic/tentative methods. Be aware that exhaustive method is ideal for evaluating naturalness, but infeasible in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative/iterative arrangement by obvious similarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators typically 'tentatively arrange' objects according to their most obvious similarities and refine definitions as new objects are considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with conspicuous resemblances to form rudiments of classes, then reassign and alter definitions as deeper similarities are discovered (historical example: development of chemical classifications; early grouping by visible metallic properties later refined by chemical analogy). Expect early classifications to break down and require revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcate classification (logical necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every superior class should be divided into two inferior classes, distinguished by the possession and non-possession of a single specified difference; this 'bifurcate' form is logically perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure classifications as a series of binary (present/absent) splits so correlations become explicit. Be aware the bifurcate form implies certain combinations do not exist (i.e., when you divide A into AB and AC you imply B and C never coexist within A). Use caution interpreting multi-way divisions (they imply absence of other combinations unless otherwise stated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic/logical methods to reveal correlations (Logical Alphabet)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of classification can be expressed via the Logical Alphabet: representing qualities as letters and arranging combinations to discover laws of correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reorder and group combinations symbolically to make correlations apparent (examples of rearranging eight combinations to reveal B = d or correlation between C and E). Use formal/symbolic analysis to detect non-obvious correlations among many properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification as an inverse and tentative operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is an inverse operation to induction; there is 'no royal road' and multiple tentative attempts are normally required. No general procedural rules guarantee discovery of the best arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept difficulty and fallibility: expect to make several tentative classifications, revise with new evidence, and avoid assuming a single method will suffice for complex groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical discriminations are exceptions to bifurcate form
rubrics_metrics.description: When the quality admits of numerical discrimination (e.g., number of atoms, sides, or degrees), numerical/series classification is appropriate and the bifurcate arrangement becomes needless or tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inherently numerical attributes (atomity, polygon sides, musical ratios), classify according to the natural numeric series rather than forcing binary splits. Recognise that number provides exhaustive and logically discriminating ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing classification on 'accidents' (irrelevant properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'Accident' is any quality that may or may not belong to objects and has no connexion with the adopted classification (e.g., size of a crystal, whether a substance is crystallised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude accidental features from definitions of classes; do not let incidental attributes determine grouping. Example anti-patterns: using absolute size or temporary state (solid/liquid/gas) as class-defining criteria when they are not correlated with deeper relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of Genus, Species, and Difference (Five Predicables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus = group defined by common qualities; Species = portion of genus distinguished by a 'difference' (an additional quality). Difference is interpreted in intension only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define genera by shared qualities sufficient to separate them from other classes, then subdivide by single differences to form species. Be mindful of intension (qualities composing definition) vs extension (set of objects included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and use 'Property' and 'Peculiar Property'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Property' is a quality belonging to the whole class but not entering its definition; a 'peculiar property' belongs to the whole class and only to that class (enabling identity statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify properties that follow from class membership (e.g., opposite angles equal for parallelograms) and highlight peculiar properties that uniquely characterise a class (e.g., circle maximises area for given perimeter). Use such properties to test and validate classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for classifications enabling deduction and prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable classification permits inference of other phenomena (e.g., knowing a crystal's primary form allows approximate certainty about thermal, optical, and elastic properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate classifications by their explanatory and predictive power: prefer those that connect form to other physical/mechanical properties and allow successful predictions (e.g., Mitscherlich's and Savart's results).
